data.title: FBI investigates apparent breach of nationwide crime database used by police
data.description:
A seal reading "Department of Justice Federal Bureau of Investigation" is displayed on the J. Edgar Hoover FBI building in Washington, DC, on August 9, 2022.
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its nationwide criminal information database that serves as a lifeline between federal, state and local law enforcement, two people briefed on the investigation said.

The intrusion of the National Crime Information Center by apparent hackers is the second such breach in recent months.

Related article
The logo of the Federal Bureau of Investigation is displayed on a building in Washington, DC, on November 28, 2025.

FBI arrests cybersecurity executive in major hack on agents’ data

4 min read

The NCIC database is used by law enforcement nationwide to share information on warrants and background checks.

The discovery of the latest intrusion in recent days comes as the Trump administration has sought to assuage public concern about the nation’s cybersecurity amid a series of high profile outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA’s air traffic control system.

The FBI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

On Thursday, after bureau officials learned of the latest cybersecurity incident, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News to tout the FBI’s cybersecurity work.

Patel used the appearance to discuss an operation completed months ago aimed at urging companies to update their systems and prevent hackers from getting to their sensitive data.

Patel referred to Operation Winter Shield as if it was still in the works, and touted the current administration for making updates to key systems to protect the nation’s critical infrastructure.

“Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t,” he said. “We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.”

The NCIC database is one of the most critical information-sharing systems in law enforcement, a former FBI official who led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN. “Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety. My concern isn’t simply whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”

Prior hacks

A September attack by a group called ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.

A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author has been arrested and faces charges related to the ShinyHunters breach.

After the ShinyHunters breach, some FBI employees felt left in the dark about whether they were affected by the data theft and underwhelmed by the security resources being offered to victims, CNN previously reported.

In an earlier breach in 2023, hackers breached a computer system the FBI’s New York field office used in child sexual exploitation investigations, including a system used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported.

CNN’s Sean Lyngaas contributed to this report.

data.title: Storms on East Coast and atmospheric river in California may disrupt Thanksgiving travel
data.description:
Thanksgiving travel forecast: Storms on the East Coast and an atmospheric river in California could disrupt travel for millions

Forecasters are monitoring a storm system offshore the southeastern U.S. that could develop into Tropical Storm Kyle.

Kate Murphy
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 8:52 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Forecasters are monitoring a possible late-season Atlantic tropical storm that could disrupt travel along the East Coast ahead of Thanksgiving.

A cluster of low-pressure systems just offshore the southeastern U.S. has a 40% chance of developing into a tropical depression or storm over the next seven days, according to the National Hurricane Center's 1 p.m. ET Friday update.

NHC forecasters say the system's development and path remain uncertain. "Regardless of development, strong winds, dangerous surf, rip currents and coastal flooding is expected along the southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts this weekend," the NHC wrote in a Friday post on X.

Advertisement

"The timing of this storm could be especially disruptive for people getting an early start on Thanksgiving travel," according to AccuWeather meteorologist Haley Taylor. "Heavy rain could move into some of the busiest travel corridors in the Northeast Sunday night and linger into Monday morning, creating difficult driving conditions. Even if the storm stays offshore, coastal communities could still experience impacts, so small changes in its track will make a big difference in what travelers encounter."

This year, AAA projects that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday, Nov. 24, and Monday, Nov. 30, including 72.9 million traveling by car and 5.96 million taking domestic flights.

Flooding concerns grow in Florida

More than 16 inches of rain fell near Cocoa Beach, Fla., over a 72-hour period ending Thursday, according to AccuWeather. Additional heavy rain could trigger flash flooding, as the St. Johns River near Cocoa reached 18.6 feet on Friday, surpassing the 17.55-foot record set in 1953.

"One area of low pressure was forming along the northeast coast of Florida on Friday," AccuWeather meteorologist Brett Anderson said. "The storm will continue to produce heavy rain on northeast Florida, spreading into coastal Georgia through Friday night, and then into South Carolina Saturday to Saturday night."

Heavy rain and strong winds threaten the Carolinas

The Carolinas face a tropical storm threat from Saturday into Sunday, according to AccuWeather. 

Heavy rain and wind gusts of 40 mph or greater could affect the Carolina coastline beginning Saturday morning. 

Coastal North Carolina could see wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph, potentially causing power outages and coastal damage. 

A storm surge of about 1 to 2 feet could affect coastal areas of eastern Florida and the Carolinas.

Travel disruptions along the I-95 corridor

Heavy rain could spread from the southeast into the mid-Atlantic on Sunday, reaching the Northeast by Monday morning and potentially disrupting early Thanksgiving travel.

Travelers along the I-95 corridor from Washington, D.C., to Boston could encounter flooded roads and delays. Wind gusts could also reach 40 to 60 mph in southeastern New England.

New York City officials said Thursday that they had activated the city's Flash Flood Emergency Plan ahead of the rain and wind storm that could bring 1 to 3 inches of rain and 30 to 40 mph wind gusts.

Atmospheric river threatens California travel

Meanwhile, on the West Coast, heavy rain from an atmospheric river could slow Thanksgiving travel along I-5 in Northern and central California, with the greatest impacts expected Tuesday and Wednesday. The storm could also trigger flooding and mudslides.

Heavy snow in the Sierra Nevada could also complicate travel across mountain passes, with possible restrictions and closures.

"Drivers along I-5 should prepare for heavy rain that can reduce visibility and leave water collecting on the roadway," according to Taylor. "Travelers heading into the Sierra will face a different challenge, with heavy snow potentially making mountain routes difficult or impassable."

Forecasters advise travelers to check updated forecasts before departing.

data.title: Chip stocks are crashing like it's 2008 as the Nasdaq finishes just shy of bear market
data.description:
Chips suffer worst week since 2001 as the Nasdaq nears a bear market

Jared Blikre
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 3:23 PM CST 4 min read
  • ^GSPC -3.70%
  • ^NDX -5.61%
  • ^IXIC -5.28%

Wall Street is wrapping up a kind of week it has seen only five other times since World War II. Two of them came in 2008 and 2001.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC) fell every day this week, with four drops of 1% or more. That had happened only in 1962, 1974, 1978, the week after the 9/11 attacks in 2001 and October 2008, according to Bespoke Investment Group.

Friday brought the sharpest leg down. The S&P 500 fell nearly 4% and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) more than 5%, wiping out the Nasdaq's gain for 2026. The S&P 500 shed about $2.4 trillion in market value on the day and closed in a correction, 10% below its Oct. 6 record, for the first time since April 2025.

The Nasdaq 100 (^NDX) finished just shy of a bear market, or a 20% drop from its record closing high. Meanwhile, chip stocks had their worst week since the one after the 9/11 attacks.

The strange part is the timing. This was supposed to be a showcase week for AI. Nvidia's (NVDA) first report since Jensen Huang's exit showed revenue more than doubling, and Anthropic (ANT) pulled off the biggest IPO ever. Both stocks sank anyway.

Read more: How to protect your money during turmoil, stock market volatility

Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value since its Oct. 6 top, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. Broadcom (AVGO), Micron (MU) and AMD (AMD) each fell about 12% to 14% Friday alone. A Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks lost about $1.5 trillion on the day, and the reasons keep piling up.

Chips are reliving 2008

The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) fell about 17% this week and has lost a third of its value since Sept. 30. That puts chips on track for their worst two months since late 2008, a pace topped only in the dot-com bust and the financial crisis. Chips hit their financial-crisis low 18 years ago to the day, on Nov. 20, 2008.

The Nasdaq 100 and the tech sector are on the same track. The S&P 500 is headed for its worst November since 1973, and the Nasdaq for its worst since 2000. The S&P 500 has given up about $8 trillion since its record, nearly $6 trillion of it this week.

The rest of the market isn't

That's where the 2008 comparison breaks down. In October and November 2008, the typical S&P 500 stock lost about 28%. This time, the equal-weight S&P 500 (RSP) is about flat since Sept. 30.

Walmart (WMT) and Costco (COST) are rising Friday. A Goldman Sachs version of the S&P 500 that leaves out AI stocks is only about 5% below its record, Jim Bianco noted.

"I hate that comparison," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James Investment Management, said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang, when asked whether this looks like 2000. "The fundamentals are so diametrically different from where we were in 2000," adding, "The market today is healthy."

History offers some comfort, with a catch

A year after those five losing weeks in prior years since World War II, the S&P 500 was higher four times. But the next month was rough in two of them, and after October 2008 the index fell about 25% more before bottoming in March 2009.

With half of S&P 500 stocks still above their 50-day moving averages — a short-term gauge of market trend — BTIG's Jonathan Krinsky isn't ready to call a bottom.

"It would be unprecedented to be putting in a final low here with half of the SPX still above the 50 DMA."

Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.

data.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the 2025 Palisades Fire that killed 12 people
data.description:
Palisades arson retrial ends with conviction of man accused of sparking deadly wildfire

Brittny Mejia
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 11:06 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Following a mistrial over the summer, a federal jury on Friday convicted a 30-year-old former Uber driver accused of intentionally setting a blaze that later became the most destructive wildfire in Los Angeles history.

Federal prosecutors accused Jonathan Rinderknecht of using a lighter to ignite the Lachman fire on Jan. 1, 2025 — a fire they said burned underground for days and reignited as the deadly Palisades fire. Rinderknecht's defense attorney argued there was no evidence proving his client set the fire and offered fireworks as an alternate cause.

The jury deliberated for just over two days before returning its verdict of guilty on both counts he faced.

Advertisement

Rinderknecht was being tried for a second time, after a federal jury in June deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal. U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang ordered that there be no reference to the first trial and instructed the second jury to disregard a defense witness' mention of it during his testimony.

Despite the jury's lean toward acquittal over the summer, prosecutors vowed to retry Rinderknecht, who has remained in custody since his arrest in October 2025. Earlier this year, prosecutors obtained a revised indictment that narrowed the scope of one charge to focus solely on damage from the initial Lachman fire, while a second count still sought to hold him responsible for both the Lachman and Palisades fires.

The secondary inferno erupted on Jan. 7, 2025, killed 12 people, destroyed 6,500 structures across the Palisades and Malibu, and caused billions of dollars in damage and insurance claims.

Rinderknecht's second trial was contentious, with prosecutors accusing a defense witness of perjury, the defense attempting to introduce a new witness at the eleventh hour to bolster their theory of fireworks, and constant sniping between the two sides.

In closing arguments Wednesday, Assistant U.S. Atty. Mark Williams told jurors that Rinderknecht was "mad at everything and frustrated" when he hiked to a clearing overlooking Pacific Palisades and set a fire on New Year's Eve 2024. Williams said investigators ruled out fireworks as a cause "because there was no evidence to prove it."

"This fire was an incendiary fire started by an open flame," he said. "The defendant is the only one who could have started it ... He was angry that night and he set the fire and watched it burn."

Williams also reminded the jury that they were not to consider the adequacy of the Los Angeles Fire Department's fire suppression efforts, something jurors raised following the June mistrial. In a civil lawsuit against the city and the state, Los Angeles firefighters testified about a series of communication failures and questionable decisions by higher-ups that led crews to leave the area of the New Year's Day fire prematurely.

"This case is about arson, the fire that the defendant started — not about first responders who responded to it," Williams said.

In his closing argument, Steve Haney, Rinderknecht's defense attorney for both trials, said jurors were "to decide the case based on the evidence" not on anything his client did "outside of the act of arson." He argued that no one saw his client start the fire and that the ignition wasn't captured in thousands of photos and videos reviewed by investigators.

Haney said investigators concluded in August 2025 that an open flame started the fire. Rinderknecht was charged that October, but Haney said authorities didn't request lab tests to prove a lighter could have ignited the fire until the following year.

"The decision came first, the test came 11 months later," Haney said. "Decided, charged and tested. That's backwards."

data.title: Trump threatens 'tremendous tax' on tech companies that build AI centers overseas
data.description:
1. Tech
  2. General

Trump threatens U.S. companies that build data centers in other countries as Americans increasingly oppose the facilities in their communities

Plus, answers to the most important questions about the high-tech facilities that have become a major flashpoint in American politics.

Mike Bebernes
Reporter
UpdatedFri, November 20, 2026 at 8:27 PM UTC
Add to Preferred Sources
UpdatedFri, November 20, 2026 at 8:27 PM UTC
In this story:
  • What are data centers?
  • Why do we need data centers?
  • How many data centers are there?
  • How many more are being built?
  • Why do we need so many more data centers?
  • How have opinions on data centers changed?
  • Why have data centers become so controversial?
  • How much power do they use?
  • How do they affect utility rates?
  • How much water do they consume?
  • How many jobs do they create?

    • President Trump on Friday threatened to impose a "tremendous tax" on U.S. tech companies if they build data centers in other countries. 

    In this story
    • What are data centers?
    • Why do we need data centers?
    • How many data centers are there?
    • How many more are being built?
    • Why do we need so many more data centers?
    • How have opinions on data centers changed?
    • Why have data centers become so controversial?
    • How much power do they use?
    • How do they affect utility rates?
    • How much water do they consume?
    • How many jobs do they create?

    "We're gonna fight very hard for the data centers," he said at a press conference Friday morning. "We're not gonna allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country."

    The president did not provide any specifics on how the tax plan might work and told reporters that he hadn't even informed members of his own administration of his intention to implement it. 

    Advertisement
    Advertisement

    Trump has been a persistent advocate of data center construction throughout his second term, calling the facilities a "Golden Goose" for the U.S. economy. That stance puts him at odds with the views of most Americans. Recent polls show that a strong majority of those surveyed oppose a new data center being built in their communities, while only a small percentage strongly support the idea. Even Republican voters are largely against data centers.  

    A few years ago, the typical American hardly ever thought about data centers. But they've become a major political issue seemingly overnight. We've seen local lawmakers lose their jobs over their support for new data center projects. Debates over the facilities were also a key pivot point in the midterm elections earlier this month, with exit polls showing that strong majorities of voters opposed having one built in their communities.  

    Lawmakers from both parties have responded to the dramatic shift against data centers by ramping up efforts to slow down, or even block entirely, data center construction. In July, New York became the first state to ban new data center projects. Similar proposals have been put forward in more than a dozen other states. 

    There has also been momentum in Congress behind plans to rein in data centers nationwide. One of those proposals, the Ratepayer Protection Act (RPA), passed through the House in a near-unanimous vote in September, but has been stalled in the Senate ever since. 

    Advertisement
    Advertisement

    The RPA would compel state utility regulators to consider adopting a federal standard under which large data centers would cover the extra costs of upgrades. Several senators have pushed for separate legislation that represents much more aggressive efforts to curb data center-related utility costs. That includes a proposed bill that would empower federal regulators to force tech companies to cover certain costs that come from connecting their data centers to the grid. 

    A separate bipartisan bill, the GRID Act, would go even further by requiring all new data centers to have their own independent power supply that's completely separate from the public grid. Progressive lawmakers Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have called for a full, nationwide moratorium on new data centers "until strong national safeguards are in place." 

    All this is happening at a time when the president and the country's biggest tech companies are saying that the U.S. needs to dramatically increase its data capacity in order to build the economy of the future. 

    With that in mind, here are answers to some of the most important questions you may have about data centers, including why we need them, why thousands more are being built and what it means for local communities when a new data center comes to town.  

    What are data centers?

    Data centers are often called the "physical infrastructure of the internet." They are facilities where the servers, networking equipment and storage systems that allow digital data to be processed, stored and transmitted are housed. 

    Why do we need data centers?

    At a fundamental level, the modern internet simply cannot exist without them. Every email, social media post, video or news article that you can find online runs through a data center. 

    How many data centers are there?

    There are an estimated 3,000 data centers currently operating across the United States, according to a Pew analysis of industry data published in April. The facilities aren't evenly distributed, though. Virginia has nearly 400, while data centers in some states number in the single digits. 

    How many more are being built?

    There are roughly 1,500 new data centers in "various stages of development" nationwide, according to Pew. Other estimates suggest there could be as many as 3,000. But that doesn't just mean more of the same types of facilities that already exist are being built. Some of the proposed data centers are much larger than anything that's currently in operation. According to the power market tracking company Clearview, the biggest active data center in the U.S. has a power capacity of 750 megawatts. A single data center that's been proposed in Utah would have an estimated capacity of nearly 9,000 megawatts. 

    Advertisement
    Advertisement

    Data centers aren't just getting bigger. They're also being built in new places. Right now, the vast majority of active data centers are in urban areas, according to Pew. More than two-thirds of the incoming data centers will be in rural areas. 

    Why do we need so many more data centers?

    The more we ask the internet to do, the more computing power is needed to meet our demands. 

    Over the course of the past two decades, the U.S. has had to steadily build more and more data centers as so many aspects of our lives have moved online. But the recent, dramatic increase in data center projects isn't being driven by the spread of social media, the rise of streaming or the remote work revolution. It's being driven by AI.

    AI works by processing huge data sets to learn, adapt and make predictions in a way that typical algorithms can't. That takes a lot of processing power. The kind of processing power that America's data infrastructure simply won't be able to handle as AI becomes more complex and widespread, without a massive increase in data center capacity. 

    Advertisement
    Advertisement

    Tech companies are pouring money into building more data centers to support their lofty AI ambitions, which many see as a world-changing technology that will be at the core of everything we do. One estimate found that it could take $6.7 trillion in global data center investment before the end of the decade to create the scale of computing power that's needed to support AI's continued growth. 

    How have opinions on data centers changed?

    Data centers have been around in some form as long as computers have. Until recently, most Americans had no real strong opinion about them, if they were aware of their existence at all. But public opinion has shifted dramatically against data centers over a remarkably short period of time, as people across the country are being faced with the prospect of having one built in their back communities. 

    The share of Americans who say they would strongly oppose a new data center near where they live more than doubled, growing from 24% to 55%, in the span of just nine months, according to a June poll by Heatmap. Other surveys have shown that a strong majority of Americans do not want data centers built in their communities. 

    Anti-data center sentiment has been especially intense in areas where they're being built. There's a growing list of local lawmakers who have been voted out after approving the construction of new facilities. A recent study tracked the creation of hundreds of new local Facebook groups with more than 400,000 total members dedicated to bringing residents together in opposition to proposed data centers in their communities.

    Why have data centers become so controversial?

    There are many reasons people cite for why they oppose data centers. The most prominent concerns center around the amount of resources the facilities consume. Data centers use up a ton of electricity and need a lot of water to keep all those servers from overheating. 

    Advertisement
    Advertisement

    New facilities are also massive construction projects, which bring all sorts of disruptions to communities while they're being built — road closures, construction noise, huge trucks clogging up streets and more. 

    Many data center critics say it's just unpleasant to live near one. One of the main complaints is noise, which some residents have described as like having a "freight train" constantly running past their homes. Researchers have found that large data centers can have a "heat island" effect that makes the surrounding area noticeably hotter. 

    Broader skepticism of AI is also a big factor. Tech companies have argued that the U.S. needs to build all of these new data centers to support their vision of an AI-powered future. But more Americans say they expect AI to have a negative impact on society when you account for how it will affect the labor market, education, environment and our personal relationships. It's a tough sell to ask people to tolerate the downsides of having a data center in their community when they don't want the products that the facilities are being built to support.

    Finally, there's the phenomenon commonly known as NIMBYism. The acronym, which stands for Not In My Back Yard, is often used derisively to describe people who say they support the construction of things our society needs — affordable housing, power plants, prisons and public transportation — but refuse to accept those things being built where they live. In the eyes of some proponents of data centers, local opposition to building them is a classic case of NIMBYism in action. 

    How much power do they use?

    A lot. In 2024, data centers accounted for 4% of all power consumption in the United States. With so many facilities being built, the total amount of electricity data centers consume is projected to more than double by 2030, according to estimates from the International Energy Agency. A separate study estimated that data centers could account for up to 12% of all power usage in the U.S. by 2028. 

    Advertisement
    Advertisement

    A typical newly built "hyperscale" facility can require as much power as 100,000 households. The largest data centers can consume more energy than entire major cities, and demand is higher in places with the most facilities. In Virginia, for example, data centers consumed 40% of the state's electricity in 2024, according to a Bloomberg analysis. 

    Utility companies have also spent billions building out transmission lines and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the local power grid and building new power plants to meet increased demand. 

    How do they affect utility rates?

    It's important to note that all of the tangible information we have on data centers and energy prices is based on what's already been built. At this point, experts can only estimate what will happen when all of those new proposed facilities eventually begin operating. 

    That said, there's already evidence that the data centers that are currently online have had an impact on electricity rates, thanks to a combination of higher operational costs for utilities and increased demand. 

    Advertisement
    Advertisement

    Residential power rates have roughly doubled over the past 10 years. How much data centers are to blame for that increase is the source of significant debate. Some recent analyses have found that states with the most data centers have seen their energy rates climb at a faster rate than the national average. But another study suggested that their impact on electricity bills has been modest — at least so far.

    Some in the energy and tech industries even argue that data centers can actually lower energy prices. While there's some evidence to support that claim in certain areas, most experts believe the large-scale buildout of data centers across the country will push prices higher in the long run. 

    A variety of solutions have been proposed to keep that from happening, including forcing data center companies to pay for any new infrastructure or plants that utilities have to build to power them, charging the centers higher rates than typical consumers and even requiring data centers to have their own on-site power plants.  

    How much water do they consume?

    Data centers use water to keep the thousands of servers and other equipment they house from overheating. One estimate found that the typical non-hyperscale data center uses about 300,000 gallons of water per day, about as much as 1,000 U.S. households. Newer, larger facilities can use as much as 5 million gallons every day. 

    Advertisement
    Advertisement

    In total, data centers used up an estimated 66 billion gallons of water in 2023, according to an analysis by the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. That same study estimated that data center water demand could double by 2028.

    While that is a lot of water, it's a relatively small share of the 117 trillion gallons the United States uses every year, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. 

    There are also ways to significantly reduce the amount of water data centers use. Historically, most data centers relied on what's known as an open-loop cooling system, in which water is brought in, then evaporated to cool the air around servers. While that's the cheapest way to prevent servers from overheating, it's also very inefficient. There are other, closed-loop approaches that allow facilities to reuse water, which can cut a data center's water demand by up to 70%.

    More than half of all global data centers still rely on open-loop systems, but some of the biggest companies in the tech industry, including OpenAI, have said they plan to prioritize closed-loop facilities moving forward.  

    Advertisement
    Advertisement

    That change only addresses the water that data centers use directly. The facilities also impact water supplies in a larger way through their electricity consumption. The vast majority of power plants in the U.S. use water to keep their own systems from overheating. As a result, the extra strain that data centers put on electricity providers accounts for an additional 800 billion gallons of water consumed annually, according to Lawrence Berkeley Lab. 

    OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has tried to appease concerns about water usage, telling the Sources Podcast in September that data centers use no more water than an office building and that 38,000 ChatGPT queries use as much water as the production of one almond. It's a claim that many experts feel is difficult to verify given the limited amount of public information made available by AI companies and the number of vairables at play when trying to acuurately analyze each data center's water usage.

    How many jobs do they create?

    Like any major construction project, a new data center creates a lot of short-term jobs while it's being built. But once it's completed and operational, the facilities take a relatively small number of people to keep them running. The average data center creates between 100 and 200 permanent full-time jobs locally, according to a recent study by the Brookings Institution. 

    Of course, data centers don't only affect employment at the local level. The entire U.S. economy relies on the existence of infrastructure that allows us to consistently and reliably send information over the internet. At a very basic level, we need data centers. The questions of how many we need, where they should go and who should bear the costs are where the real debate lies.

data.title: Stocks continue steep dive as AI worries fuel punishing sell-off
data.description:
Stock market today: Dow and S&P 500 enter correction, Nasdaq sinks 5% to erase 2026 gains as AI trade melts down

Updated Fri, November 20, 2026 at 1:58 PM PST 1 min read

US stocks tanked on Friday as a punishing sell-off deepened after Anthropic's (ANT) successful initial public offering failed to quell broad uncertainty about artificial intelligence safety and financing.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) dropped 1.9% after the blue-chip index fell below 50,000 and neared a correction. The S&P 500 (^GSPC) declined by 3.6%. Both the Dow and S&P 500 closed in correction territory, or more than 10% off their peaks.

The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) fell nearly 5.3%, with the tech-heavy index closing negative for the year.

Investors went risk-off on Friday as semiconductor stocks led an AI trade sell-off. Nvidia (NVDA) shares extended losses, falling 14%. AMD (AMD), Broadcom (AVGO), and Micron (MU) stocks also suffered double-digit drops.

Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre finds the damage beneath the Nasdaq Composite index is even worse. Seventy-one of the 101 stocks in the narrower Nasdaq-100 (^NDX) were in bear market territory on Friday, including 20 of the 20 semiconductor and memory chip stocks in that index.

A day after its record-breaking debut, Anthropic shares fell 8%, though they remain narrowly above their IPO price of $83. After a big pop on its IPO day, Anthropic faces a test in the markets to see whether it can sustain the momentum.

data.title: The next Senate has 98 names. 2 incoming governors can fill in the final blanks.
data.description:
The last big midterms mystery: Who will these future governors choose to replace them in the Senate?

Minnesota's Amy Klobuchar and Tennessee's Marsha Blackburn will have the power to personally select their successors when they're sworn in to their states' top office.

Mike Bebernes
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 7:43 PM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The last undecided Senate race finally got a winner on Tuesday night when Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan to give her party its ninth flipped seat this midterm cycle. 

Peltola's win, which came more than two weeks after Election Day, means the final balance of power in the Senate is set. When the new Congress convenes for the first time in January, Democrats will control 56 seats, and Republicans will hold 44 seats. 

But there are still two important questions that remain unanswered about the next Senate caucus. As it stands, we only know the identities of 98 of the 100 senators who will serve in the upcoming Congress, and it could be weeks before we find out who those last two pivotal lawmakers will be. 

Advertisement

That's because two current senators, Tennessee Republican Marsha Blackburn and Minnesota Democrat Amy Klobuchar, were each elected governor of their home states. They will need to leave the Senate to assume their new positions. 

Laws in Tennessee and Minnesota give governors the power to temporarily fill Senate vacancies. That means Blackburn and Klobuchar can each choose their own successor as one of their first acts as governor if they wait to resign from the Senate until shortly before they're sworn in. Both have indicated they plan to do so but have offered very few clues about who they might consider. 

It's highly unlikely that either of them would select a replacement from the opposition party, so the partisan split in the Senate probably won't change. But their decisions will still carry a lot of weight. Whoever they choose will occupy two of the most important legislative seats in the U.S. government and could play a significant role in defining the ideological direction of their respective parties. 

Volunteers in Tennessee

Blackburn, who has represented Tennessee in the Senate since 2019, announced her bid for governor in August 2025, just nine months after winning reelection to a second Senate term. This year's gubernatorial race was much closer than Republicans in the Volunteer State are accustomed to, but Blackburn was still able to defeat her Democratic challenger, Jerri Green, by more than 50,000 votes. She is the first woman elected to the state's top office. 

Blackburn is a staunch conservative and Trump ally. She opened her first gubernatorial campaign video by saying, "Trump is back. America is blessed and Tennessee: better than ever." Her MAGA credentials suggest she's likely to select a successor with a similar profile, but that won't be certain until her choice is formally announced. 

Throughout the campaign, Blackburn repeatedly declined to answer questions about who she might choose to replace her but said early on in the process that she intended to make the decision herself, rather than leaving it up to outgoing Republican Gov. Bill Lee. 

That hadn't changed in the weeks since she was formally elected. She told Fox News on Nov. 15 that she hadn't made up her mind and didn't yet have a "short list" of potential replacements. 

"I'm focused on finishing the work in the Senate and transitioning to governor," she said.

Blackburn's coyness hasn't stopped speculation about who her selection might be. In the days after Democrats' decisive midterm performance earlier this month — which many top Republicans attributed to voters' dissatisfaction with the war in Iran — rumors began to spread that Blackburn might choose embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to fill her seat. Those rumors were quickly refuted by sources close to Blackburn. 

The two names that have been most frequently suggested as Blackburn's replacement are former Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs and U.S. Rep. Tim Burchett. 

Jacobs turned to politics after a long career in professional wrestling, where he performed as the horror-themed character Kane. He told Fox News in September that it would be a "huge honor" to be Blackburn's chosen successor and he would "consider it very seriously" if asked. 

Burchett, who represents Tennessee's deep red Second District in the House of Representatives, has said he "absolutely" wants to be considered for the position. He has also made clear that he intends to run for the Senate in 2028 against Blackburn's pick if she chooses someone other than him. 

Blackburn is scheduled to be sworn in as governor on Jan. 16 and would likely appoint her replacement shortly after taking office. Whoever she chooses will hold her seat until the 2028 general election, when a special election will be held to decide who will finish out the remaining two years of her term. 

A battle brewing in Minnesota

When Minnesota's Democratic Gov. Tim Walz abruptly dropped his bid for a third term in January, reports immediately began to circulate that Klobuchar was considering launching a bid to replace him. She made it official a few weeks later. A former presidential candidate with a strong record of success in statewide races, Klobuchar quickly became the frontrunner in the Minnesota governor's race. She easily defeated Republican Lisa Demuth on Election Day. She will be the first woman to serve as governor of her state as well when she's sworn in on Jan. 4.

Like Blackburn, Klobuchar has said she intends to choose her own successor and has remained mum on who she may be considering. One name that can be crossed off the list is Walz, who said he would "rather eat glass" than take over her Senate seat. 

Under Minnesota law, Klobuchar's successor would fill her seat on a temporary basis until November 2027, when a special election will be held to decide who will finish the remaining three years of her term. Because of that short time frame, Klobuchar has described the appointment as an "interim position."

"It would be for about a year," she told a local news station last month. 

Nothing in Minnesota law bars appointees from running to keep their seat, but there is some recent history of governors filling vacancies with lawmakers who promise not to campaign for reelection. 

Replacements often end up holding on to their seats, however. Minnesota's other senator, Tina Smith, was appointed to her seat in 2018 and has been reelected twice since then. Smith is retiring when her term ends in January.

Klobuchar could insist that her successor pledge to serve only as a temporary placeholder, but she hasn't said whether she might disqualify potential candidates who decline to do so. 

Her selection, and the Senate race that will follow in November, could say a lot about the ideological direction of the Democratic Party. Midwest swing states were home to some of the most tightly contested midterm primary battles between progressive and moderate candidates anywhere in the country.

Minnesota's Senate primary was won by the more left-leaning candidate, Peggy Flanagan. The same thing happened in nearby Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed eked out a primary win over moderate Haley Stevens. Both Flanagan and El-Sayed won their general election races earlier this month.

data.title: Trump defends calling Putin a friend but won't say if he's a friend to the U.S.
data.description:
Trump defends calling Putin a friend but says he ‘can’t speak’ to whether he's a friend to the US

BILL BARROW and BEN FINLEY
Updated Fri, November 20, 2026 at 6:24 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump doubled down Friday on his description of Vladimir Putin as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether the Russian president is a friend to the U.S.

Trump also insisted during a White House news conference that Putin wants peace with Ukraine, despite Russia's continued aggression after invading more than four years ago. Asked about the most recent attacks — hours after Putin met with Trump in China — Trump suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Putin share equal responsibility for the ongoing conflict.

"He'd love to end the war," the U.S. president said of his Russian counterpart. But, "you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other, Zelensky and Putin. They don't know how to end it. They want to end it. They're both stuck in it."

Advertisement

During a wide-ranging news conference, Trump praised both Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping after returning from China, where he participated in bilateral and trilateral meetings with his fellow heads of state.

Trump raised eyebrows on the trip with his warm welcome and repeated references to Putin as his "friend." He made no effort in the White House briefing room to walk back the comments. And he noticeably sidestepped a specific question about whether he views Putin as a friend to the United States.

"I can't speak to America," Trump said, without expounding.

He shifted immediately to his "very good" personal relationship with Putin and repeated longstanding grievances over the extended federal probe that concluded that Russian agents sought to influence U.S. voters in the 2016 presidential election on Trump's behalf.

"I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with)," Trump said. "It's actually very good."

"I've been dealing with Putin" since "the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax," as Trump calls the Department of Justice investigation. "It was a hoax made up by the Democrats" and "probably helped me win," Trump said.

Trump insisted his relationships with the other world leaders is key to an eventual peace.

"You know, you're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who stood on stage during Trump's news conference and made brief remarks, echoed the president's sentiments, pushing back against criticisms that Trump was embracing autocratic leaders as trusted allies.

"I want everybody to understand the relationships between heads of state are invaluable," said Rubio, who traveled with Trump to Asia. "It sets the tone for the entire relationship. It sets the tone for our trade negotiators. It sets the tone for our diplomats." __

Barrow reported from Atlanta.

data.title: Trump threatens 'tremendous tax' on tech companies that build AI centers overseas
data.description:
US tech companies that build AI data centers in other countries will be penalized, Trump says

Associated Press
Updated Fri, November 20, 2026 at 5:45 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. tech companies will face "a tremendous tax" if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries, President Donald Trump said on Friday.

Trump did not provide details and said he hadn't yet told his own officials about his plan. The Republican president urged Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities and extract concessions from the developers, repeating a point he made before the midterm elections.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centers," Trump said in a White House press briefing. "Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don't shut them off."

Advertisement

The Republican-led Senate on Thursday approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation's energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if Trump — perhaps the industry's biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.

Despite backing from Trump, the data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom have become politically toxic.

The tech industry says it has gotten the message. Besides ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build.

Companies are also making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values — all while maintaining AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its skeptics.

With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America's technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China's abilities to use U.S. chips to train its best artificial intelligence models.
